lessons.title: From HTML to a real page
lessons.heading: 01  /  HTML becomes a webpage
lessons.html:
Code Club

Build. Test. Share.

Friday at 14:00.
lessons.voice: HTML describes a webpage. The head holds information about it. Title names the browser tab, not the visible heading. The body contains visible content. H one creates the main heading. P starts a paragraph. B makes Friday bold; I makes the time italic. Each closing tag belongs to its opening tag. Predict what changes if you edit only the title.
lessons.concept: A document has metadata in head and visible content in body. title names the browser tab; h1 is the visible main heading. Paragraph and formatting tags change the displayed content. Closing tags nest in reverse order.
objectives: Distinguish head, title and body in a working HTML file.
Explain heading levels, paragraphs, bold and italic formatting.
Connect one source region to the corresponding browser region with native editable motion.
lessons.htmlExercise: Create a Music Club page. Keep a valid document skeleton. Set the tab title to Music Club, the h1 to Friday Sessions, add two paragraphs and use b and i in one paragraph. Predict and verify what changes when you edit only title. Save it as index.html, not index.html.txt.
lessons.creativeExercise: Use your own page recording. Move the two editable focus outlines to your actual code and browser heading, then replace the four callouts with concise explanations. Keep the whole 16:9 source visible. Add one original label using Graphics → Label; position it in the reserved footer.
questions: If title changes to Music Club but h1 stays Code Club, what changes?
The document/tab title changes; the visible h1 stays Code Club. They are separate elements.

Why does

Friday

need repair?

The elements are improperly nested. Close b before p:

Friday

. Browser error recovery is not a substitute for correct source.
Does h1 simply mean “make text big”?
It identifies a top-level heading. Default browser styling makes it large; heading hierarchy communicates structure.
criteria: Correctly distinguish metadata and visible body content (4).
Use valid skeleton, paired/nested tags and meaningful headings (4).
Predict a title-only change and verify actual browser behaviour (4).
Keep code/output readable; focus outlines point to matching evidence (4).
Recreate native timing/position changes and justify a creative choice (4).

lessons.title: Images, attributes and working links
lessons.heading: 02  /  Attributes connect the page
lessons.html:
Club gallery

About the club
lessons.voice: Attributes add information inside an opening tag. S R C tells the browser where to find the image. Alt describes its content. A wrong path can break the image; the alternative text still describes it. Check the filename and folder, then reload the correct file. H ref gives the link destination. Click About the club: the browser really opens about dot H T M L.
lessons.concept: An attribute is a name/value pair inside an opening tag. img is a void element: src selects an image and alt supplies a text alternative. a uses href to select a destination. Relative paths resolve from the current document location.
objectives: Explain src, alt, width and href using a working local website.
Diagnose a deliberately incorrect image path and verify the corrected result.
Show the code/output relationship with timed native highlights and callouts.
lessons.htmlExercise: Create your own original image and a second page. Use a relative src, useful alt text and a relative href. Break the image path deliberately, record expected/actual output, correct it, and test the hyperlink. Explain why alt is not normally drawn on top of a loaded image.
lessons.creativeExercise: Record the broken and corrected browser cases. Retarget the code/output outlines to your own coordinates. Use a contrasting callout for the error and a calm colour for the fixed result. Keep the working hyperlink click in the source evidence.
questions: Is alt a tooltip that always appears on the picture?
No. It is a text alternative, including for assistive technology and unavailable images; title is a separate attribute with different behaviour.
Why can club.svg load but Club.svg fail?
Paths can be case-sensitive on the hosting filesystem. Verify exact case, extension and folder. Local tolerance does not guarantee hosted success.
Does clicking a link upload the target file?
No. The browser follows its URL. The target must already exist at the resolved location.
criteria: Use a working image with meaningful alt and explain src (4).
Show broken-path diagnosis plus a successful retest (4).
Test the actual local hyperlink and explain href (4).
Align timed highlights and narration with real browser evidence (4).
Recreate and adapt callout coordinates without obscuring content (4).

lessons.title: Lists, tables and readable design
lessons.heading: 03  /  Give information a structure
lessons.html:
Club plan

  • Code
  • Test
DayTask
FriBuild
lessons.voice: Use a list for items and a table for related data. U L creates an unordered list. Each L I is one item. Change U L to O L to number the items. A table contains rows. T H marks header cells; T D holds data. Here Friday matches Build. Keep the reading order clear. Border equals one is legacy classroom syntax; modern sites normally style borders with C S S.
labels: ul + li: a group of items
lessons.concept: ul and ol express unordered and ordered lists; li is a list item. A table organises related data into rows and cells. th provides header cells, td data cells. Logical order, readable labels and purposeful formatting support good webpage design.
objectives: Choose unordered versus ordered lists for the intended meaning.
Relate table rows, header cells and data cells to the browser output.
Explain a readable visual design and distinguish legacy CAT attributes from modern CSS practice.
lessons.htmlExercise: Create a club event page with an ordered setup checklist, an unordered equipment list and a table with two columns and three data rows. Use useful headers. Diagnose an intentionally missing closing table tag by inspecting source and actual browser DOM; do not assume every malformed tag causes an obvious visual error.
lessons.creativeExercise: Use a native outline to follow one list item, then one table row. Place a short explanation in the footer. Change its arrival easing and explain whether the slower movement makes the correspondence easier to follow. Include a readable pause at each endpoint.
questions: When should ol replace ul?
When the sequence or ranking matters, for example instructions. Unordered lists represent items whose order is not meaningful.
How many cells are in the example table?
Four: two header cells and two data cells, arranged as two rows and two columns.
Is border="1" modern HTML styling?

It is legacy presentational syntax retained for this CAPS-oriented classroom comparison. Modern standards-based sites use CSS; ask the teacher which syntax the current tag sheet and assessment require.
criteria: Choose list type correctly and nest li elements (4).
Build consistent rows and correctly related headers/data (4).
Explain data structure, diagnose source and test a new case (4).
Use readable spacing, contrast and logical visual order (4).
Recreate native keyframes and explain a purposeful design choice (4).

lessons.title: Headings give a page its structure
lessons.heading: 04  /  Make the hierarchy clear

files.index.html:
Science Club

Weekly plan

Build, test, share.
files.flat.html:
Science Club

Weekly plan

Build, test, share.

phases.label: h1: the main heading
phases.voice: H one identifies the main heading. It gives the page a top level.

phases.label: h2: a section beneath it
phases.voice: H two marks a section below it. Heading levels communicate structure, not just size.

phases.label: b, i and u change presentation
phases.voice: B makes text bold. I makes it italic. U underlines it. Use each choice deliberately.

phases.label: Spot the lost heading level
phases.voice: Now both headings use H one. The levels look the same. Explain what changed.

lessons.concept: HTML heading levels express hierarchy. h1 is a top-level heading and h2 a subordinate section heading. Bold, italic and underline affect presentation; they do not turn paragraph text into a heading.
objectives: Connect h1 and h2 to a meaningful heading hierarchy.
Distinguish heading structure from bold, italic and underlined text.
Use native outlines and timed callouts to compare a working page with a deliberately flattened hierarchy.
lessons.htmlExercise: Create a Science Fair page with one clear h1, two h2 section headings and a paragraph under each. Use b and i purposefully. Compare the DOM and browser after changing one h2 to h1. Explain why larger text alone does not make a good hierarchy. Do not use underline merely to imitate a hyperlink.
lessons.creativeExercise: Record your original and flattened heading examples. Retarget the native source/output outlines to your headings. Keep the hierarchy comparison readable and add one original short callout in the reserved footer. Explain how its timing supports the concept.
questions: Is bold paragraph text equivalent to h2?
No. b changes presentation; h2 identifies a heading level in the document structure.
Does the file break when h2 is changed to h1?
It can still render. The example loses the intended top-level/subordinate distinction; this is a structural/design problem rather than necessarily a loading error.
Why can an underlined word be confusing?
Readers may expect underlined text to be a link. Underline by itself does not add href or navigation.
criteria: Use an appropriate main heading and subordinate sections (4).
Explain structural headings versus presentational formatting (4).
Predict and verify a heading-level change in real HTML/browser output (4).
Keep focus outlines/callouts readable and correctly placed (4).
Recreate and adapt native timing/key values for a different page (4).

lessons.title: Design for the person reading
lessons.heading: 05  /  Make the page easy to use

files.index.html:
CODE CLUB WORKSHOP!

Friday 14:00 laptop beginners welcome

Click here
files.clear.html:
Code Club

Friday workshop

Bring a laptop. Start at 14:00.

Read the workshop plan
files.plan.html:
Workshop plan

14:00: Build a simple webpage.

14:30: Test it with a partner.

Back to the club

phases.label: Low contrast hides useful details
phases.voice: Pale text on white hides the workshop details. This is a deliberately poor design.

phases.label: Readable text comes first
phases.voice: The revised page uses readable dark text. The time and equipment are easy to find.

phases.label: Hierarchy helps a reader scan
phases.voice: A main heading, a section heading and a short paragraph give the information a clear order.

phases.label: Say where a link will take you
phases.voice: Read the workshop plan describes the destination. Click it, then check the actual page.

lessons.concept: Good webpage design helps a reader find and use information. Readable contrast, purposeful heading hierarchy, concise content and descriptive links matter. The poor example uses a legacy font attribute for a classroom contrast comparison; modern sites normally style colour with CSS.
objectives: Identify a readability problem in actual browser output.
Explain how contrast, hierarchy and concise content improve a page.
Use a native before/after explanation and a real link test to support a design decision.
lessons.htmlExercise: Improve the deliberately poor index.html. Make the important information readable, organise it with meaningful headings and replace the vague link label. Test the linked page. Explain each decision. The font tag in the poor example is legacy classroom syntax; ask your teacher which syntax the current tag sheet requires, and distinguish it from modern CSS styling.
lessons.creativeExercise: Build a brief before/after explanation from your own page. Use one caution-coloured callout for the fault, a calm colour for the improvement and measured native outlines around the corresponding source/output. Keep all original content visible; make the final link test genuine.
questions: Does colourful text automatically improve a webpage?
No. Colour must preserve readability and serve a purpose. Very low contrast can make information difficult to read.
Why is Read the workshop plan more informative than Click here?
It tells the reader what to expect from the destination rather than describing a generic action.
Is font color modern HTML styling?

The example demonstrates a legacy presentational attribute still encountered in classroom material. Modern standards-based websites normally use CSS. The teacher should confirm current assessment syntax.
criteria: Identify and correct a readability problem (4).
Use purposeful hierarchy, concise content and descriptive links (4).
Test the real destination and justify the design decisions (4).
Make the before/after comparison and focus regions accurate (4).
Recreate the edit and explain how motion/colour aid communication (4).

lessons.title: Find the fault, fix it, retest
lessons.heading: 06  /  Follow the evidence

files.index.html:
Code Club

Workshop details
files.fixed.html:
Code Club

Workshop details
files.details.html:
Workshop details

Friday at 14:00 in the lab.

Bring your HTML file and test it.

Back to the club

phases.label: Read the reference exactly
phases.voice: The link names details dot H T M. Check that exact filename before guessing.

phases.label: 404: the requested file is missing
phases.voice: Click the link. That file is missing, so the browser reports a not-found error.

phases.label: Match the actual filename
phases.voice: The supplied file is details dot H T M L. Correct the reference and save it.

phases.label: Retest and check the destination
phases.voice: Retest the corrected link. The right page loads. Record expected and actual results.

lessons.concept: Troubleshooting follows evidence: reproduce the problem, compare the reference with the actual filename, change the cause and retest. Here details.htm is missing while details.html exists. The .htm extension is not inherently invalid; either extension can work when it matches a real file. The video uses a local HTTP server and a genuine 404 response; a file:// browser session may instead show a local file-not-found message.
objectives: Reproduce a genuine missing-file error through an actual hyperlink.
Distinguish a filename mismatch from an inherently invalid extension.
Show the correction and successful retest using real source/browser evidence and native motion.
lessons.htmlExercise: Run index.html and reproduce its broken link. Record the requested path, expected destination and actual response. Correct href so it matches the supplied file, then retest. For a second test, create a real file called extra.htm and link to it. Explain why that .htm link can work.
lessons.creativeExercise: Explain the fault/correction/retest in three purposeful stages. Retarget the native outlines, use a caution colour only for the failed case and keep the actual click and corrected destination in the source. Add a short prediction prompt without covering the code.
questions: Are all .htm links wrong?
No. Both .htm and .html can be valid filenames. This example fails because the referenced file does not exist at that path.
Why should you click the link after changing href?
Changing source alone does not prove the issue is resolved. Retest the actual navigation and confirm the intended destination.
What belongs in the test table?
The test/action, expected result, actual result and outcome. Keep the original failed case, the correction and the successful retest as distinct evidence.
criteria: Reproduce the missing-file error and identify the exact reference (4).
Correct the filename mismatch and explain extension validity (4).
Retest the real link and record expected/actual outcomes (4).
Align the source/output highlights and error/correction stages accurately (4).
Recreate the native edit and justify a useful prediction prompt (4).

studioSteps.title: Retain the teaching audio
studioSteps.control: Captions → Preview captions off; Sound → Keep original audio on → Use voice repair on export off
studioSteps.value: No captions; original narration at 100%; no additional music or repair.
studioSteps.why: Preserve the precisely timed explanation and the clean screen source.

studioSteps.title: Import the editable teaching design
studioSteps.control: Graphics → scroll to Import graphics composition → Import graphics composition…
studioSteps.value: lesson.graphics.json from this lesson folder. Fourteen ordinary editable layers; no separate renderer.
studioSteps.why: The outlines draw on at the moments described by the voice. Every parameter is listed below.

studioSteps.title: Inspect and adapt a callout
studioSteps.control: Graphics → Title layers → callout → Copy, colour, timing and size
studioSteps.value: Callout text from the recipe; X50%, Y92%, width94%, scale0.69, colour #b7f4e1.
studioSteps.why: The reserved footer keeps the explanation away from code and browser evidence.

studioSteps.title: Follow the motion key
studioSteps.control: Motion → Transform keyframes → Target layer → Stroke end → Curve keyframe
studioSteps.value: Select Code focus 1. At 0s Stroke end=0; at 0.7s Stroke end=100; arrival easing Ease In Out.
studioSteps.why: A native editable outline draws around the actual source region.

studioSteps.title: Add a label manually
studioSteps.control: Graphics → scroll to Add title layer → Label → Copy; Motion → Target layer → X/Y
studioSteps.value: Use the exercise label text. Set X50%, Y84%; width60%; size0.55; start24s; duration4s.
studioSteps.why: This demonstrates original authoring rather than only importing a starter design. Save a separate exercise copy.

studioSteps.title: Review and export the lesson
studioSteps.control: Play → Save project → Export → Render Final Clip → Download
studioSteps.value: 720p; 24fps; H.264/AAC MP4; complete28s. Wait for completion off camera, then show the complete finished playback.
studioSteps.why: Download the actual native export and retain the editable owned backup.
